mcqs.question: Why is a bonus "target" percentage not the same as a guaranteed payout?
options: The target assumes both company and individual performance hit 100%, so the actual payout is usually a range around that figure, not a floor
Bonuses are only paid if the employee requests them in writing each year
Target bonus percentages are renegotiated every quarter
Bonus targets are only paid to employees rated in the top 10%
mcqs.explanation: A bonus target is the number you'd get if company and individual performance both hit exactly the plan — actual payouts commonly land above or below that depending on both factors, so it should be modeled as an estimate, not a guarantee.

mcqs.question: In a standard 4-year vesting schedule with a 1-year cliff, what happens if you leave the company at month 11?
options: You receive whatever percentage the stock price has changed since your start date
You receive a prorated 11/12 of the first year's vest
You receive the full first-year 25% vest early as a departure bonus
You receive zero equity, since nothing vests until the cliff is reached at month 12
mcqs.explanation: The defining feature of a cliff is that nothing vests at all until the cliff date — leaving even one month early means walking away with none of the first year's equity, regardless of the grant's headline size.

mcqs.question: Why should private-company equity get a much steeper valuation discount than public-company RSUs when converting a grant to an annualized estimate?
options: Private companies pay a lower tax rate on equity grants
Private equity carries the added risk that the company never reaches a liquidity event at all, unlike public stock which already has a realized market price
Public RSUs vest over a shorter period than private equity
Private equity grants are always smaller in absolute share count
mcqs.explanation: Public RSUs already sit at a real, tradeable price, so the discount is mostly ordinary volatility; private equity's headline value depends on an exit that may never happen, which is why many candidates model it at a fraction of face value absent a concrete near-term liquidity path.

mcqs.question: Two offers both show "$250k total comp," but one is a public company with RSUs and one is a startup with options at last-round valuation. What's the correct way to compare them?
options: Take both totals at face value since they're both officially stated by the company
Always choose the startup offer, since options have unlimited upside
Risk-adjust the equity portion of each — discounting the illiquid, exit-dependent options far more than the liquid RSUs — before comparing the resulting expected totals
Ignore equity entirely and compare only base salaries
mcqs.explanation: The headline totals look identical only because both count equity at face value; applying a realistic risk discount to the illiquid startup options (and a much smaller one to the liquid RSUs) reveals the two offers are not actually equivalent in expected value.

mcqs.question: Why can a large one-time sign-on bonus make an offer look better than it really is when comparing multi-year total comp?
options: Companies that offer sign-on bonuses never offer competitive base salaries
It inflates the year-one total while contributing nothing to years two through four, distorting a comparison that only looks at a single year or a single averaged total
Sign-on bonuses always come with better health benefits attached
Sign-on bonuses are never taxed, unlike base salary
mcqs.explanation: A sign-on bonus is a one-time payment concentrated in year one; averaging it across multiple years or comparing only headline year-one totals overstates the offer's ongoing value relative to an offer with a higher recurring base or equity refresh instead.

mcqs.question: In the worked example, why is year-one total comp meaningfully lower than the naive headline average of base plus bonus plus equity?
options: Sign-on bonuses are taxed at double the normal rate
The bonus isn't paid until year two in this example
The base salary in year one is prorated for a partial year
The 1-year vesting cliff means zero equity vests in year one, even though the naive average assumes a steady equity amount every year
mcqs.explanation: The naive average spreads the equity grant evenly across all four years, but the cliff means the real year-one equity vest is zero — that gap, not the bonus or sign-on, is what makes the naive headline number overstate year one specifically.
